web_title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
question: Is the market confirming the business story, or is the stock still in a decline that the price has not yet left?

web_blocks.html: The business story is in chapters 2 to 6. The tape answers a narrower question: is anyone paying for that story today? On 13 November 2026 the answer is not yet. Stallion closed at ₹187.12 after a fall of 5 percent on the day, on volume about 2.7 times its 30-day average [32]. The stock is up 36 percent over six months, down 21 percent over three months, and 33 percent below its 52-week high of ₹279 [32]. That is the shape of a stock that ran hard, then began to give the gains back, and has not yet found a floor.

On our classification the stock is in Stage 4. In the Weinstein framework a Stage 4 stock is in decline, trading below its long-term averages, and the discipline is not to buy it until it has built a base and broken out again. The company-specific snapshot agrees: it classifies Stallion as STAGE_4 with the posture AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN, and it applies a technical ceiling of CAP_REJECTED [32]. We carry that classification into the decision in chapter 9. We have not overridden it.

web_blocks.takeaway: The price is under six of the seven averages. The 200-day average at ₹182.89 is the only one it holds above, and that is why the 200-day line features in the levels and options sections below.

web_blocks.html: The momentum readings agree with the averages. Daily RSI is 40.6, weekly RSI 46.1 and the 4-hour reading 37.7. Readings below 50 mean sellers have had the upper hand on each timeframe, and the 4-hour reading is the weakest. The 4-hour close of ₹187.12 sits below its 20-period average of ₹196.71 [32]. Average true range over 14 days is ₹10.26, about 5.5 percent of the price, so a normal day is wide enough to shake out an entry placed carelessly inside the zone.

web_blocks.title: The day, the week and the quarter

web_blocks.html: The one-day fall of 5 percent on 2.7 times normal volume is the reading we weigh most heavily. A quiet drift lower on thin volume is ordinary. A sharp fall on heavy volume can mean sellers are taking size off the table, or that the stock is being repriced after news. The data we reached do not say which. We did not find a delivery-percentage or block-deal series for the session, so we cannot tell whether the volume came from long-term holders or from short-term traders [32].

Over one week the stock fell 8.2 percent, over one month 11.3 percent and over three months 20.7 percent. The six-month gain of 36 percent is still large. The pattern is a sharp run-up followed by a retreat that has not yet stopped. Among the three peers in chapter 7, the snapshot places FLUOROCHEM in Stage 2, NAVINFLUOR in Stage 2 awaiting a pullback, and SRF in Stage 4, the same as Stallion [33][34][35]. Stallion is not the only fluorochemical stock in trouble on the tape, but it is one of only two of the four in decline.

No-FOMO means we do not chase. An entry is allowed only when the stock is inside its support zone, the zone holds on a closing basis, and the short-term structure starts to repair. The table applies that test to the data as it stood at the close on 13 November.

web_blocks.takeaway: Four gates fail, one is not yet reached, the volume gate points the wrong way, and one passes only marginally. The gate result is no entry today. The support zone is a level to watch, not an order.

web_blocks.html: Pivot points put the first support at ₹157.43 and the second at ₹130.89. Resistance sits at ₹224.86 and ₹265.75 [32]. Our support zone of ₹155.07 to ₹159.79 sits on the first pivot, which is why the zone is a level the market has already used rather than an arbitrary number. The invalidation stop at ₹152.30 sits just below it. A weekly close under ₹152.30 would mean the support had failed, and a break through the zone could carry the price to the ₹130.89 pivot, about 18 percent below the zone top. The weekly-close rule accepts that path. The next structural level down is the ₹130.89 pivot, about 30 percent below today's price.

Above the price, the first obstacle is the 50-day average at ₹209.16, with the 10-week and 30-week averages between ₹201 and ₹203 just under it. A weekly close back above that band, on volume above the 30-day average, would start to repair the damage. We would not call it a Stage 2 breakout on one close. It would need to hold for several weeks, because a single close above a falling average in a downtrend often fails.

web_blocks.title: Institutional flow: what we can and cannot see

web_blocks.html: We can see price, volume against its average and the position against the averages. We cannot see delivery data, changes in institutional holdings or block trades for this session from the sources we reached. Promoter holding fell from 67.90 percent to 47.80 percent between September 2025 and March 2026 [15]. A change of that size is a fact the flow question has to carry, even though the filings in our record do not explain its cause. We treat the flow evidence as incomplete. We do not claim institutional selling or buying.

The options snapshot labels the price a DISLOCATION_AT_MAJOR_SHELF, meaning it has moved well away from its averages toward the 200-day line, and it says the repair is not yet confirmed [32]. Stallion is not in the NSE derivatives segment, so there is no options chain behind that label. It describes the price structure only. The live TradingView review that normally confirms the chart was also skipped in this run, so this reading has not been checked against a live chart.

We would move the tape reading up if three things happened in order: a weekly close back above the 30-week average at ₹201.15, a 4-hour close above the 20-period average at ₹196.71, and a daily close above the 50-day average at ₹209.16 on above-average volume. We would move the call toward rejection if a weekly close fell under ₹152.30, which is the invalidation level used in chapter 9. The tape does not settle the business question. It settles the timing.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: A chart cannot tell you why a stock fell. It can tell you whether the market has stopped selling. For Stallion the answer today is that it has not. The price is under most of its averages, the momentum readings are weak on every timeframe, and the one day of heavy volume points down.

That is the reason the entry sits in a zone rather than at the current price. The zone is where the company's own history and the market's own structure first meet, and the stop sits just beneath it so that the mistake is small if the zone fails.

book_paragraphs: Now the tape. I want to be clear about what it can and cannot tell you. It is a record of what buyers and sellers agreed to pay in the last few months. It does not know whether the plants will work. It does tell you whether the crowd is paying for the story right now, and on 13 November the answer is that it is not.

The price closed at 187.12 rupees after a fall of about five percent on the day. Volume was about 2.7 times its usual level. A large fall on heavy volume is a different thing from a quiet slide. It can mean holders are reducing exposure, or it can mean the stock is being repriced after news. I could not find the delivery figures that would separate the two, so I hold that question open.

The averages tell the same story. The price is below the 10-day, 20-day, 50-day, 30-week and 10-week averages. It is above the 200-day average at 182.89, and that is the one long-term line still under it. Stage 4 is the label for a stock in that position, and the rule for a Stage 4 stock is simple. Do not buy it until it has built a base and broken out again.

I use a no-chase rule, which means no entry until the stock is inside its support zone and the zone holds. For Stallion, the support zone is 155 to 160 rupees, and the stop is 152.30. The price is about 17 percent above the top of that zone today. So the gate says no, and that is the answer I would give you whether or not I liked the business.

The levels come from the market's own structure. The first pivot sits at 157.43, inside the zone, and the second at 130.89 is the next structural floor if the first gives way. Above the price the obstacles are the 50-day average at 209 and the weekly averages just under 203. A repair would need a weekly close back above that band, on volume, and then it would need to hold.

Flow is the hardest part to see. I can read price and volume, but I cannot read who is trading. Promoter holding fell from about 68 percent to about 48 percent in six months. The filings I read do not explain why, and I have not claimed an explanation. A change that large should make you careful about the story the company tells, not because it is false, but because you have not yet seen the reason.

It helps to know the vocabulary. A Stage 1 stock is building a base after a decline. A Stage 2 stock is advancing, trading above a rising long-term average. A Stage 3 stock is topping out, and a Stage 4 stock is declining below a falling average. The working rule is to buy in Stage 2 and avoid Stage 4. That is simple to say and harder to apply, because a change of stage is only clear after it has happened. That is why this dossier waits for a zone to hold rather than predicting the bottom.

The 200-day average is the line I watch most closely here. At 182.89 rupees it is the one long-term average the price still sits above. It is a useful reference because it summarises roughly a year of trading. A close below it would turn a slow decline into a break of support, and that would make the zone at 155 to 160 more important, not less.

The 4-hour readings are the short-term instrument. They show whether a bounce is being bought or sold into. Here the 4-hour close sits below its 20-period average, and the 4-hour RSI at 37.7 is the lowest of the three timeframes. A stock that bounces on the daily chart while the 4-hour chart keeps falling is usually a stock where sellers use each rally to reduce, not one that has turned.

The volume reading needs care. Heavy volume on a down day is not, by itself, proof that large holders are leaving. Stocks fall on news, and the volume can simply reflect the repricing. What matters is what comes next. If the following sessions show volume drying up on down days and rising on up days, the message changes. If they show heavy selling into every rally, the message is the same as today's: the stock is still being sold.

The pivot levels deserve a note of their own. Pivots are calculated from the prior session's high, low and close, so they are mechanical, and that is both their strength and their limit. Traders watch them, which can make them self-fulfilling in the short run. The first pivot at 157.43 sits inside our zone for that reason. A break through it would tell you that the market, not just the formula, has stopped defending the level.

I would not trade a pivot on its own. I would use it as one of several lines that agree. Here the first pivot sits inside the support zone, and the zone lies well below the 40-week average at 190.51. Reaching it would mean a larger break of the recent trend. That is exactly why it is a useful place to test the stock, and also why it is not a promise that the price will hold.

So the tape is not a sell signal, and it is not a buy signal. It is a timing signal, and right now it says wait. Chapter 9 weighs that against the business and the price, and it puts numbers on the wait.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Before you act on any chart, write down the level that would prove you wrong. For Stallion that is a weekly close under 152.30. If you cannot name the level, you are not analysing the stock. You are hoping.
